title: Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes of Sequential Full-Endoscopic Decompression Followed by Adjunct Interspinous Stabilization for Grade I Degenerative Spondylolisthesis: A 1-Year Retrospective Study
content: Introduction: Full-endoscopic decompression has shown favorable outcomes for lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) with Grade I degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis (DLS); however, concerns remain regarding postoperative segmental instability and slip progression. This study evaluated the clinical and radiographic outcomes of sequential full-endoscopic unilateral laminotomy for bilateral decompression (FE-ULBD) followed by adjunct interspinous stabilization. Material and Methods: We retrospectively evaluated 47 patients with symptomatic single-level LSS and Grade I DLS who underwent sequential FE-ULBD followed by adjunct interspinous stabilization between January 2022 and April 2025. Clinical outcomes were assessed using visual analog scale (VAS) scores for leg and back pain, the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and the modified MacNab criteria. Radiographic outcomes included percent slip, mean disc height, dynamic angular motion, segmental translation, and segmental instability. Radiographic progression was defined as an increase in percent slip of more than 5 percentage points at 12 months. Results: VAS scores for leg and back pain and ODI scores improved significantly (all P &lt; 0.001), and 42 patients (89.4%) achieved favorable modified MacNab outcomes. The percent slip and segmental translation showed no significant changes after 12 months. Segmental instability decreased from 36.2% to 23.4%, although the difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.146). Radiographic progression occurred in 4 patients (8.5%) and was not associated with worse 12-month clinical outcomes. Complications occurred in 6 patients (12.8%), and 4 patients (8.5%) underwent revision surgery. Conclusions: Sequential FE-ULBD, followed by adjunct interspinous stabilization, was associated with significant clinical improvement, and radiographic parameters were generally maintained over 1 year.
